title: How to design an MVP: from riskiest assumption to tested prototype
metaTitle: How to Design an MVP: Scope, Flows, Prototype, Test
metaDescription: How to design an MVP: pick the riskiest assumption, cut to one core flow, prototype that flow, test it with 5 users. Then book a free consultation.
centralEntity: how to design an MVP (designing a minimum viable product)
sourceContext: ui-ux.agency (the design team of tkxel, Reston, VA) writes as a product design team that designs MVPs for startup founders: research with target users, a cut feature list, user flows, UI, a clickable prototype tested with 5–8 users, and a build-ready handoff to developers (tkxel engineers can build it). The post explains the method a founder can follow alone and shows where a design team changes the outcome, without restating the hub's package, process or price.

serpGaps: Every ranking guide (upsilonit, purrweb, mockplus, uxtweak, uxplanet, ronasit, richux, capicua, dbbsoftware, parallelhq) lists the same generic sequence: research → features → wireframes → prototype → test → iterate. None starts from the riskiest assumption and uses it to choose the MVP TYPE (smoke test, concierge, Wizard of Oz, clickable prototype, single feature). Our decision tree fills that gap.
No guide gives a pre-design decision sheet. We add the one-page MVP brief (lead asset), filled in before any screen exists.

Scope advice stops at 'pick one core feature'. Nobody shows how to cut with a written reason per item (must / later / never) or sets a screen budget for the core flow. We add the cut board with reasons.
Wireframe sections skip screen states. An MVP's first session starts empty; nobody covers empty, loading, error and success states for the core flow.

Testing advice is 'test with early users'. No guide writes the test before the test: tasks, success thresholds and what go / change / stop means, or cites the NN/g 5-user model with its formula and its 'several small rounds' caveat. We add the test scorecard.
No page covers the US accessibility baseline for an MVP (WCAG 2.2 AA contrast 4.5:1 and 24 px targets, with ADA/Section 508 as the frame), even though fixing it later means redrawing every component.
Handoff is a single line on most pages. We list what developers need from an MVP's design files (states, specs, prototype link, decision log, open questions), linked to the hub deliverable.

Statistics on page 1 are mostly unsourced or vendor prices ($1,490–$5,600 gigs, '$1,500 to $100,000+'). We use sourced facts only (Ries, NN/g, WCAG, Figma docs, CB Insights with edition labels) and the hub's published facts by deep link.

contentModules.title: How to design an MVP: from riskiest assumption to tested prototype
contentModules.subtitle: A founder's method for designing a minimum viable product: decide what the first version must prove, pick the MVP type, cut to one flow, wireframe it with its states, set the UI bar, test with 5 users and hand developers a build-ready file.
contentModules.intro: Originator-quote intro (see variety.introStyle): open with Eric Ries's own line that the MVP 'is not about creating minimal products', then Sahar's first-person point of view on the misreading she sees (founders designing a small product instead of a small test), then the keyword sentence and the definition inside the first 60 words.

dataModules.h2: What should you decide before you design an MVP?
dataModules.what: The one-page MVP brief: 8 fields (target user, problem in their words, riskiest assumption, MVP type, core flow, must-have list, test threshold, go / change / stop action). One illustrative filled example for a hypothetical US product (see notes: EXAMPLES).

dataModules.h2: Which type of MVP should you design first?
dataModules.what: Riskiest assumption → MVP type: 'Will anyone want it?' → landing page smoke test; 'Will they pay for the outcome?' → concierge; 'Can the experience work before the tech exists?' → Wizard of Oz; 'Can users complete the core flow?' → clickable prototype; 'Will they come back?' → single-feature product.

dataModules.h2: How do you cut an MVP down to one core flow?
dataModules.what: Feature | must / later / never | the reason in one line (which assumption it serves). 8–10 rows for the hypothetical product. Introduced by one sentence and a 'Table:' line.

dataModules.h2: How do you map the core user flow and wireframe it?
dataModules.what: 4–6 screens from entry to first result, each with its empty / loading / error / success states listed underneath.

dataModules.h2: How polished should MVP UI design be?
dataModules.what: Sketch → low-fidelity wireframe → clickable grey-box → high-fidelity prototype; for each: what it tests, who sees it, rough effort.

dataModules.h2: How do you test your MVP prototype with 5 users before code?
dataModules.what: Task | success measure | threshold | result | go / change / stop. Thresholds are the founder's own, set before the sessions; no benchmark numbers invented.

dataModules.h2: What should developers get when you finish designing the MVP?
dataModules.what: Bulleted checklist in text (no separate image needed): annotated screens, all states, component specs and tokens, prototype link with flow starting points, the decision log (what was cut and why), open questions.

outline.h2: What does it mean to design an MVP?
outline.answerHint: **To design an MVP is to decide the smallest version of your product that tests one risky assumption with real users, then draw and test that version before anyone writes code.** (≤35 words)
points: Ries's definition with link (eav[0]) and his 'not about minimal products' clause (eav[1]); expand minimum viable product (MVP) on first use. Name The Lean Startup and the build-measure-learn loop in one sentence each, with a real fact (validated learning = the measure of progress).

Design vs development: design decides what the first version is and proves it on a prototype; development builds it. One sentence on why that order saves money (changes on a prototype cost hours; no invented ratio).
First UP link to the hub inside the first 300 words: 'our MVP design agency team' anchor, one clause on what it delivers (clickable prototype tested with real users). Do not list the 6 deliverables.
Bridge: 'Before any screen, one page of decisions.'

outline.h2: What should you decide before you design an MVP?
outline.answerHint: **Decide four things before you open a design tool: who the first user is, the problem in their words, the one assumption that would sink the idea if wrong, and what result would count as a pass.**
points: Why it matters: CB Insights post-mortems (eav[3]) with edition labels; no market need is a problem you test before design, not after launch. One sentence, not a stat-led paragraph.
YC (eav[4]): feature set and user tests come from talking to users first. Do not quote unverified Seibel lines ('launch a crappy MVP in 30 days' is DO NOT USE).
The one-page MVP brief (visual 1 + astext) with the illustrative filled example. This is the post's lead asset.
Carry 'design mvp' here once (keywordCarrier.secondary).
Bridge: 'The riskiest assumption also tells you what kind of MVP to design.'

outline.h2: Which type of MVP should you design first?
outline.answerHint: **Choose the MVP type by the assumption it has to test: a landing page tests demand, a concierge or Wizard of Oz MVP tests the outcome, a clickable prototype tests the flow, and a single-feature product tests whether people come back.**
points: Decision tree (visual 2 + astext). Hyponyms as H3s if needed: landing page smoke test, concierge MVP, Wizard of Oz MVP, clickable prototype, single-feature product (eav[5]).
What each type asks of design: copy and one form; a service script and a thin interface; a front end that looks real; a full core flow with states.
Answer 'Is a clickable prototype an MVP?' here in one sentence (it is one MVP type: it tests usability and value perception, not retention or payment).

When the idea itself is unproven, a 5-day design sprint comes first (pillars.ts FAQ): the post's ONE cross-hub link (/services/startups/design-sprint/). Pillar mention /services/startups/ optional here.
AI products: a Wizard of Oz MVP lets founders test an AI feature's experience before the model is ready; one sentence, no extra hub link.
Bridge: 'Whatever the type, the scope has to shrink to one flow.'

outline.h2: How do you cut an MVP down to one core flow?
outline.answerHint: **Cut an MVP by keeping only the features the core flow needs to test your riskiest assumption, and write down why every other idea moves to 'later' or 'never'.**
points: MoSCoW (eav[6]) as the known method; our variant must-have / later / never (eav[7]) with a reason per item. Feature prioritization is a decision log, not a vote.
Cut table (visual 3 + astext) for the hypothetical product, 8–10 rows.
Screen budget as the author's rule of thumb: the core flow from entry to first result fits on one storyboard; the hub illustration shows 4 screens (state as illustration, not a rule).

Common traps in reasoned bullets: login and settings before value, admin panels, notifications, 'just one more' integration, multiple user types in v1 (the hub says user types drive price; deep link the hub cost section rather than stating figures).
DOWN link: Vocable (eav[17]): scope kept tight around the jobs writers named most often; each screen tied to an interview pain point.
Bridge: 'With the cut done, draw the flow.'

outline.h2: How do you map the core user flow and wireframe it?
outline.answerHint: **Map the core user flow from the first screen to the first result, then sketch each step as a low-fidelity wireframe, including what the screen shows when there is no data, when it loads and when something fails.**
points: First sentence after the bold answer carries 'MVP UX design' (keywordCarrier.secondary).
Flow first, screens second: entry point → sign-up only if needed → setup → the action → first result. Keep steps few; each step justified by the assumption.
Low-fidelity wireframes (eav[8]): grey boxes, real words, no colors. Test the grey-box flow before visual design (hub process step 2, eav[11]) without rebuilding the hub's 4-step list.
Screen states (eav[9]): empty, loading, error, success for every core screen; the empty state is the first thing a new user sees in an MVP.
Flow storyboard with state strip (visual 4 + astext).
Web or mobile first: pick the platform where the first user does the job (FAQ covers it).
Bridge: 'Grey boxes prove the flow; then decide how finished the screens must look.'

outline.h2: How polished should MVP UI design be?
outline.answerHint: **MVP UI design should be polished enough that users trust it and judge the idea rather than the rough edges, and no more: a light brand style, consistent components, real copy and an accessible baseline.**
points: Ries's 'not about minimal products' applies to quality: viable means usable and credible; early adopters forgive missing features, not broken flows.
Fidelity ladder (visual 5 + astext): which fidelity for which test and audience (investors see the high-fidelity clickable prototype; first usability round can be grey-box).
Starter component library rather than a full design system (hub deliverable 'Interface design', eav[15]); one sentence why it speeds the build.

Accessibility baseline, US frame: WCAG 2.2 AA contrast 4.5:1 (eav[13]) and 24×24 CSS px targets (eav[14]); ADA and Section 508 as the US frame in one clause; fixing contrast after launch means touching every component.
DOWN link: Elia Wellness (eav[18]): readable layouts and big tap areas for adults over 50 on tablets.
Bridge: 'Now put the prototype in front of five people.'

outline.h2: How do you test your MVP prototype with 5 users before code?
outline.answerHint: **Give 5 target users the clickable prototype and 3 to 5 real tasks, measure each task against a pass threshold you wrote down beforehand, then decide go, change or stop.**
points: NN/g 5-user model (eav[10]) with its formula, the 31% L value and the 'several small rounds' caveat; expand Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g). Hub runs 5 to 8 users (eav[11]); say so once.
Recruit the target user from the brief, not friends; one line on screener questions.
Figma: share a link to the flow starting point (eav[12]); remote unmoderated tests with Maze (tool listed in content/home.ts) or moderated video calls.
Test scorecard (visual 6 + astext): task | success measure | threshold | result | go / change / stop. The founder writes the thresholds; the post gives no benchmark rates.
What 'change' means in practice: fix the flow and run another small round; 'stop' sends you back to the brief, not to more screens.
LEAD ANGLE lives at the end of this section (see leadAngle). One natural invitation in the 'we' voice using hub facts only.
Bridge: 'A pass means the design is ready for developers, if the file is.'

outline.h2: What should developers get when you finish designing the MVP?
outline.answerHint: **Developers should get a build-ready file: annotated screens with every state, component and spacing specs, the clickable prototype link and a short log of what was cut and why.**
points: Handoff checklist as a ul (text only, no extra image): annotated screens; empty/loading/error/success states; component specs and tokens; prototype link with flow starting points; decision log; open questions and edge cases; analytics events for the test threshold metric.

outline.h2: When does designing an MVP need a design team?
outline.answerHint: **Designing an MVP needs a design team when the test keeps failing for reasons you cannot see, when investors need a credible prototype on a deadline, or when the product has more than one user type.**
points: Reasoned bullets (situation + because): two 'change' results in a row; a pre-seed round date; marketplace or multi-role product; AI feature whose behavior must be simulated; no one on the team has run a usability test.

Timeline once: 4 to 8 weeks with a team (hub, eav[16]). Do NOT rebuild the agency vs freelancer vs no-designer table; link or mention it (hub section 'mvp-design-agency-vs-a-freelancer-vs-no-designer', conditional).
Price: do not state a number; link the hub cost section with a descriptive anchor ('what MVP design costs with our team' counts as one of the 4 allowed bare 'MVP design' uses).

Optional plain mention (no link): Nitro League, where discovery and stakeholder interviews gave the user flows and professional gamers tested the final product (nitro.md lines 74–76). Do NOT mention the $5M raise as a design result.
Answers 'how do i design my mvp without a designer?' in one sentence here or in the FAQ: yes, with this method; the risk is in testing and handoff.
Bridge to Bottom line.

faqs.q: How many screens should an MVP have?
faqs.a: As few as the core flow needs to reach the first result. Count the steps from entry to that result and design each with its states; anything outside that path waits for version two.

faqs.q: Can I design an MVP without a designer?
faqs.a: Yes. A founder can write the brief, sketch the flow and test a clickable prototype in Figma. The usual gaps are screen states, accessibility and a build-ready handoff, which is where a designer saves rework.

faqs.q: Is a clickable prototype enough for an MVP?
faqs.a: Yes, when the riskiest assumption is whether users can complete the core flow or want the result. No, when you need to know if they will pay or come back; that takes a concierge MVP or a working single-feature product.

faqs.q: Should an MVP be web or mobile first?
faqs.a: Design for the device your first users already use for the job. A B2B workflow tool usually starts on the web; an on-the-go consumer habit usually starts on a phone. Design one platform first.

faqs.q: How long does it take to design an MVP?
faqs.a: A founder can sketch and test a first flow in a few weeks. With our team it takes 4 to 8 weeks, including research, a clickable prototype, tests with 5 to 8 users and developer handoff.
MVP UX design is the part of designing an MVP that decides the user, the core flow and how the screens work, before the visual UI design. It is tested with users on low-fidelity wireframes first.

visuals.idea: A single index-card-style sheet with 8 labeled fields (target user, problem in their words, riskiest assumption, MVP type, core flow, must-haves, pass threshold, go / change / stop action), one filled in with handwriting-style text for the hypothetical product. Not the ledger ruling of saas-homepage-design or the rule sheet of user-onboarding-automation: use a punched index card with a torn edge. Text panel: the 8 fields and the example values.

Top node 'What would sink the idea if wrong?' branching down to 5 endpoints drawn as small artifact icons (landing page, person with a tray, curtain, phone with taps, repeat arrow) labeled smoke test, concierge, Wizard of Oz, clickable prototype, single-feature product. Vertical, not the horizontal pill tree of saas-homepage-design or the zigzag of design-system-roi. Text panel: the 5 routes as a list.
Three columns of sticky notes (Must / Later / Never) for the hypothetical product, each note with a one-line reason; the Must column visibly short. Text panel: the cut table.
4–6 grey-box phone or browser frames left to right from entry to first result, with a row of 4 tiny thumbnails under each (empty, loading, error, success). Text panel: each step and its states.

Four rising steps (sketch, low-fidelity wireframe, clickable grey-box, high-fidelity prototype), each with what it tests and who sees it (you, 5 users, investors). Contrast and 24 px target badges on the top step. Text panel: the four rungs.

A clipboard scorecard with 4 task rows, columns task | success measure | threshold | result (5 dots per row, one per participant) | verdict stamp (go / change / stop). Illustrative data for the hypothetical product, labeled as an example. Text panel: the columns and the rows.
